speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: TABLING OF NEW RENTAL SCALE FOR PUBLIC HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to table a new rental scale for public housing in Canada; and I suggest, if the house is agreeable, that it be appended to Votes and Proceedings.
I am not going to make an extended statement, but I think I should say that a number of provincial governments have expressed concern about the rent to income scale for public housing that has been in force in Canada without material change since 1962. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has given careful consideration to the matter, and the rent to income scale that I ask leave to table is the result. It provides for reductions in rent averaging $16 per month per unit.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that Ontario, the province most directly affected by the new scale, agrees with the new scale and proposes to introduce it; and as I understand it, the responsible minister is tabling it this afternoon in the legislature in Toronto. The new scale is available immediately to all provinces wishing to adopt it in public housing projects.

subtopic: AMNESTY TO PRISONERS DURING CENTENNIAL
AMNESTY TO PRISONERS DURING CENTENNIAL
speechtext: In view of the intended visit of Her Majesty during Canada's centennial, does the government intend to grant amnesty to prisoners in federal institutions in honour of the occasion?

subtopic: AMNESTY TO PRISONERS DURING CENTENNIAL
speechtext:
It
is not intended to recommend that amnesty be granted to prisoners in federal institutions on the occasion of the forthcoming visit to Canada of Her Majesty the Queen. Amnesty was granted to prisoners on the occasion of Her Majesty's visit in 1959. However, on that occasion the Minister of Justice stated that, as the operations of the newly established National Parole Board became effective, so that every inmate thereafter would receive detailed consideration, under the process of automatic review, as to his eligibility for release prior to the termination of sentence, it was not anticipated that a general amnesty would be considered on the occasion of visits of Her Majesty to Canada thereafter. It is to be noted that all sentences in federal institutions are now in fact reviewed automatically by the National Parole Board and paroles granted in appropriate cases. Prior to the visit of Her Majesty in Canada in 1964, the Minister of Justice at that time stated in the House of Commons that, in view of the implementation of the Parole Act, it would not be proper that an amnesty be granted on the occasion of that royal visit, and none was granted. For similar reasons, therefore, the government of Canada will not recommend a grant of amnesty in connection with the Queen's forthcoming visit to Canada.

subtopic: STUDY OF HALIFAX HARBOUR
speechtext:
I am informed by the Atlantic Development Board as follows: 1. The board has engaged consultants to carry out a study of waterfront land for industrial uses of the Halifax harbour-Bedford basin area.
2.	The terms of reference are as follows:
1.	The consultant will perform, in a manner satisfactory to the executive director, the following, hereinafter called "the project": Prepare a master plan of land use for the Halifax harbour and waterfront area, as defined in paragraph 2 hereof. For this purpose,
the consultant will: (a) examine the role and future of the port of Halifax in relation to the economic development of the Atlantic provinces and to Canada's external and inter-regional trade; (b) carry out an inventory of existing land uses in the waterfront area and assess their present and prospective economic function. This will involve an assessment of the industrial land presently available within the area and the possibilities of further development by appropriate government agencies and/or private interests; (e) estimate the approximate cost of developing various sites, including the cost of site preparation and layout and the installation of necessary services; (f) make recommendations concerning the extent and location of

subtopic: ADHERENCE BY CANADA TO UNESCO TREATY
ADHERENCE BY CANADA TO UNESCO TREATY
speechtext:
1.	Is Canada a party to the UNESCO treaty (sometimes referred to as the Florence agreement) concerning trade in educational, scientific and cultural materials?
2.	If not (a) for what reason (b) will the government give consideration to Canada becoming a party to this treaty?

subtopic: ADHERENCE BY CANADA TO UNESCO TREATY
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned: 1. No.
2. Although the Florence agreement is commendable so far as it goes, it does not provide for the removal of non-tariff barriers which are by far the most important obstacles to Canadian exports of educational, scientific and cultural materials. These barriers consist of quantitative import controls and particularly protective restrictions embodied in the copyright laws of some of our major trading partners. The agreement requires only the removal of tariffs. On this point Canada already provides duty free entry

February 8, 1967
Questions
under the Tariff Act for most of the categories of materials covered by the agreement. The remaining tariffs are quite moderate.
It would therefore be of doubtful value at this time for Canada to abandon the limited protection of the residual tariff without a corresponding reduction in the most important form of protection, non-tariff barriers, employed by other countries. The unilateral removal of these Canadian tariffs would achieve little in terms of improved access for Canadian exports of educational, scientific and cultural materials and would not confer substantial benefits to the Canadian consumer.
At the same time the importance and value of the Florence agreement as a means of furthering cultural and scientific exchanges among member countries are fully recognized and the question of eventual Canadian adherence to the agreement is kept under continuing review.

speechtext: With six and a half million tax forms to deal with each year it is inevitable that a few mistakes will be made in sending out the forms. subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at ten o'clock last night I had just time to introduce the subject with which I want to deal in this budget debate. It has to do with the role of the federal government in the financing of higher education in Canada, particularly universities. I had mentioned that the government announced in October that they were

February 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Prittie withdrawing from this field, and that I did not like that idea. I want to point out in the course of my remarks today that the federal government has a legitimate role to play in the financing of universities and that they have abdicated this responsibility.
On October 31 the Minister of Finance, speaking for the Prime Minister, made an announcement following the tax sharing agreements with the provinces. He announced that the federal government was going to leave the field of technical and vocational education and the field of university grants and was going to transfer to the provinces four points of personal income taxes and one point of corporation income tax, so that the provinces could handle these responsibilities themselves.
As I said last night they did one positive thing in their announcement in October.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. May I bring to the attention of hon. members that it is very unfair to carry on conversations in the way it is being done at the moment when a member of the house if trying to deliver a speech. I suggest that conversations that are essential and urgent should be carried out behind the curtains.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Speaking on motions on October 31 I did say that there was one positive result of the government's announcement on that day. It was announced that the government would concern itself with the field of adult education, and the following definition of "adult education" was given. I will quote the remarks of the Minister of Finance from page 9290 of Hansard of October 31:
We must recognize that rapid technological and industrial change now require more and more training and retraining of adults. This is of fundamental importance if full employment and increased productivity are to be achieved. The federal government has a responsibility for ensuring that the required training is financially possible for people in the labour force.
For this purpose, the federal government proposes to pay training allowances directly to adults who are taking occupational training, in place of sharing provincial costs as we are now doing.
A little farther on he goes on to define who adults are. He says:
Our proposal was to define an adult as one who has been three years out of school and in the labour force. Several of the provinces felt this was unduly restrictive. We undertook to discuss immediately with the provinces whether some modified definition is possible which would meet more of the training needs of people who have been in

the labour force for less than three years, while still preserving the important distinction between this training program and the school system.
I agree completely with that step. 1 think that the federal government should concern itself with the field of adult education, and indeed the job cannot be done properly in any other way. Unfortunately it has taken a very narrow view of the word "education" as it is carried on in the regular institutions of learning such as elementary and secondary schools, universities, community colleges, and so on. It seems to me a very narrow point of view and one which cannot be defended.
As I have stated in the past, one can reasonably argue that the federal government has a role to play in the field of university financing. The move which the government made is wrong on two counts. It gave the provinces too great a control of the universities. I think it is a healthy thing that universities in this country should receive their money from several sources. They receive money from the provincial governments, they receive some money from the federal government, and they receive money from private sources. Furthermore they still collect, unfortunately, a great deal in student fees. I believe that if the universities of this country are to have the type of independence which they should have, their revenues should come from several sources so that no one source can have complete control over the educational institution. I realize that universities cannot be completely independent; all educational institutions have to respond in some way to the society which they serve. However, they should have as much independence as is possible, and I do not think this can be achieved if they receive all their money from one source.
The difficulties from too great a provincial control have been borne out since the government statement at the end of October. We have the example of McGill University in Montreal. This university is not receiving from the province of Quebec the amount of money which it feels it needs to operate during the next year. I do not blame the province of Quebec. They may have very good reasons for not taking out of their provincial revenues and giving to McGill as much money as that university requires. The educational responsibilities in that province are very great at the present time. It is trying to build new universities and colleges and to establish new institutes of education. However, the important point here is that McGill is not just a provincial institution. It does not just serve
February 8, 1967

the province of Quebec. It serves all of Canada. A great many of its students come from other provinces. It has specialized graduate schools to which people must come if they want that kind of education in Canada. So the point here is that McGill is a national institution serving the whole country, and therefore it should receive some of its funds from the whole nation.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
My second point is in connection with my own province, British Columbia. Just the other day the premier of the province, who is also the provincial minister of finance, announced that the three universities in British Columbia will receive $53 million next year for their operating and capital building costs. Now, the president of the University of British Columbia, Dr. John B. MacDonald has said that the three universities would require as a minimum $66 million for the coming year. Under the transfer of funds which is to take place from the federal government to the provinces by means of the transfer of certain taxes, British Columbia will get for university purposes about $28.6 million during the next year. I do not know whether the provincial government is going to apply all of that to the universities of the province. It may be that they are, and it may be that they are not; I do not know. The point is that the grant is unconditional. There is no guarantee that once a province receives that money the universities will get their share. Here we have the universities of British Columbia that are going to be short $13 million this year at a time when enrolments are rising, when they are in competition with universities all over the world for staff and when they can look forward to increasing enrolments in subsequent years.
As I have pointed out in past debates, a very good case can be made for federal involvement in higher education, that is at the university level. I have stated in the house in the past that when the Fathers of Confederation used the word "education", they probably meant the type of education which existed in Canada at that time and which was mainly primary school education. We did not have very many high schools in Canada in 1867, and very few colleges and universities. Most of the schools were primarily of the one room, country school type. I am sure the Fathers of Confederation did not have in mind higher education because there was virtually none in existence in the country at that time, very few institutions.
The Budget-Mr. Prittie [Translation]

speechtext: Laval University.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, it is exactly that.

I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the University of Laval existed, McGill and some others, but there were not many.
It is always interesting when you can get some good, academic support for the point of view you are trying to advance. I should like to quote rather extensively today, Mr. Speaker, from a speech made by Dr. J. A. Corry, principal of Queen's University and which was published in "University Affairs", December, 1966. This speech was delivered in October, just at the time of the federal-provincial tax-sharing conference. The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) was to have spoken at that meeting, but Dr. Corry had to take her place. He said his views were probably different from those of the Secretary of State. In this case, I am very glad the Secretary of State could not speak because I very much like the views outlined by Dr. Corry. I want to quote rather extensively from this speech because I believe these views do constitute support from a very distinguished academic for the role of the federal government in education:
Let us look at first principles. On first principles, where should the responsibility for education rest in a federation? The answer is not easy.
May I interject to say that is probably the understatement of the year: The answer is not easy.
On the one hand, any denial in 1867 of provincial control of education in and for the province would have made a mockery of plans for ensuring provincial autonomy. No community, then or now, can ensure its life or mould its future unless it has the say on education in that community. In any vital federal system, the province must be able to shape the main features of education in and for the province.
On the other hand, if there is indeed a nation to be spoken for and protected, then the federal government-
Again, I interject, Mr. Speaker, to add that the word "nation" as Dr. Corry has used it is the ordinary meaning of that word in the English language. I realize this may be different from the way it is used in French. He speaks of the nation, the state or the country.
On the other hand, if there is indeed a nation to be spoken for and protected, then the federal government must speak for the nation, take steps to ensure its survival and nourish its growth. If the nation is also a living community, it cannot be shut out of all influence on the direction of education. At times, it may be that mere adding up

February 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Prittie
of the educational effort of ten provinces will give a sum that covers federal concern in education. At other times, it will not, and then parliament and the government of Canada must have the power to give special emphasis and some direction to selected aspects of education. When that emphasis and direction will be needed must depend on the exigencies of particular times.
I continue quoting from another part of the speech:
Let us look at this matter in the widest possible frame. The training of the militia, a citizen army, is a form of education. In 1867 the Fathers of Confederation did not hesitate to confer that authority on the federal parliament because a sturdy trained militia might well be vital to the security of the nation. Today, when a sturdy militia, whether well trained or not, seems largely irrelevant other forms of much more sophisticated skill are vital to the nation. At any rate, the arguments of the Economic Council of Canada are fully convincing to me and I shall not rehearse them here.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the following sentence is, I believe, a most important one in Dr. Corry's speech.
In the competition of nations for power, place and welfare, the prizes are going to the countries that bet on education. Can the body responsible for the peace, order and good government of Canada blandly assume that ten provincial governments, each thinking for itself and about its own needs, will produce all the highly educated skills that are needed? The government of Canada, on mandates given to parliament by the people of Canada undertakes a wide range of complex functions, many of which call for civil servants with a great variety of skills. Does the government of Canada do its duty if it fails to make sure that enough people acquire these skills?
I will not quote the next paragraph in the speech which has to do with the bilingual responsibility of the federal government. The inference is that this should be a proper concern of the federal government in bilingual education. This is an idea that I heartily support, but I will omit that paragraph at the moment. I am very glad that the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) is here because he has a great interest in these matters, and I think he will want to listen particularly to the next paragraph.
But it will be asked, does not section 93 of the British North America Act give exclusive power over education to the provinces? This is correct, subject to a limitation that is likely to become more portentous as time goes on. Literally, the words of section 93 are, "in and for each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education." If there are national needs and objectives that require concerted educational policy in two, several, or all provinces, no provincial legislature is by itself competent in the matter, and judicial interpretation on other comparable aspects of the distribution of powers under the British North America Act makes it clear that parliament is competent under "the peace, order and good government" clause.

It must be on this ground that Prime Minister Pearson, in his proposal to the federal-provincial conference now meeting asserted federal jurisdiction in the training and retraining of adults for participation in the labour force. It is to be hoped that a reading of this particular assertion along with other general disclaimers in the text of his proposal about federal authority in education will not give rise to inferences that the federal government has neither status or lively concern in the education of highly skilled and highly educated manpower in the universities. It would be incongruous to be asserting federal authority over training for run-of-the-mill jobs in the labour force and abandoning it totally for all professional, scientific and technical personnel educated by the universities. It is the latter who will be critical for national objectives in the future.
At a time when the federal government is attempting to make clear that it has a constitutional responsibility for adult retraining programs, for research, and for cultural development, and that these are not, constitutionally speaking, educational matters falling within the jurisdiction of the provinces, from which the federal authority is excluded, I think it timely to recall that in 1867 none of the newly formed provinces regarded university and college education as being a matter for provincial jurisdiction. All the universities then existing (including my own) operated under royal charters or other non-provincial authority. Since then provincially supported institutions have developed but these were not considered to be the exclusive responsibility of the provinces. Indeed it is worth noting that McGill University and Queen's University, to name only two, were in the habit of appealing from time to time to business, industry and individual benefactors on the grounds that they were private institutions catering to a national (and in some respects international) constituency.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
It is only within very recent years, since the provinces have provided immensely increased support for universities that they have become concerned to exercise substantially increased control. To the best of my knowledge no province has yet claimed exclusive jurisdictional control. Universities and colleges are free to solicit funds from business, industry, foundations and benefactors inside and outside the province, inside and outside Canada. Most provinces in addition are prepared to accept a federal concern and the federal government should be reluctant to disclaim its concern.
I feel that this federal concern is there and should be exercised by the federal government.
Federal concern, Mr. Speaker, does not mean complete federal control. Regardless of its recent announcement the federal government will continue to provide some finance for universities. For example, through agencies such as the National Research Council, the Defence Research Board, the Canada Council and the Humanities Council funds do pass from Ottawa to universities across the country. But it seems to me that it is very artificial to separate this aspect of research
February 8, 1967

from the general field of university education, particularly graduate education.
I feel that there should be some agency here in Ottawa which will concern itself with this whole field of university education and post-graduate education as well as with general grants for research. If we are afraid of appellations like "department of education" or "office of education", we do not have to use them. We could call such a body a department of science and technology. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that Dean Bladen in making his report on higher education in Canada recommended that all of the agencies in the federal government concerned with making grants to education should be responsible to one minister. This recommendation is to be found at page 67 of the Bladen report.
I now come, Mr. Speaker, to this question: Why did the federal government take the stand it did and say that it would concern itself with adult education for people who have been out of school for three years, but that it would forget about existing universities? I think this decision was taken particularly as a result of the advice given to the government by the so-called three wise men who entered the Liberal party a year ago. I am not using those words sarcastically in referring to the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier), the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand); they are all very intelligent men.
However, Mr. Speaker, these hon. members are trying to develop the theory that all of the provinces should be on exactly the same footing as the province of Quebec. For example, if there is any objection from Quebec to there being a federal concern in a certain field, then they contend the federal government should have nothing to do with that particular field. Hence they are saying to the other provinces that Quebec is withdrawing from a certain program or a certain field, and they put all provinces on the same basis.
They are arguing, Mr. Speaker, against the case which others have made during the past few years that Quebec is not a province like the others. I would agree, Mr. Speaker; I think Quebec is not a province like the others. It is a different case and we should recognize this. The very fact that Quebec has a very large language group, which carries with it its own culture, does make that province different from the others. If Quebec has to be dealt with differently in some aspects of national policy, then let us recognize this fact.
23033-810J
The Budget-Mr. Prittie
Even the United Kingdom, which is not a federal state but a unitary state, recognizes it must deal with different language groups. Take the case of Scotland. If by mistake you asked a Scotsman from which part of England he came, then you should stand back and wait for the blow. The same is true of the Welshman. This difference is recognized in the United Kingdom. Scotland has a different type of educational system from England. The British Broadcasting Corporation operates a separate Scottish service and in Wales even broadcasts in the Welsh language. Scotland has its own laws. So as I say, Mr. Speaker, the United Kingdom does recognize this fact. The parliament of Westminster, of course, makes laws for the whole of the United Kingdom; but there is recognition that the people who live in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are different from those who live in England and in some respects, including education, require different treatment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there would be no great objection from most of the provinces to a continuing federal role and federal concern in university education. This concern may be directed through a government department, or could be handled in the way university grants were handled previously, through the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. If this is the best way then perhaps we should use that channel.
If there is a vital objection from the province of Quebec to a certain proposal then we can make a special case and treat that province differently. But it seems to me that the government is moving in the wrong direction. At a time when, as Dr. Corry has pointed out, the prizes in the world go to the best-educated nation, it seems to me that we must move in the direction of some type of federal concern. I am using the word "concern" deliberately and not the word "control". I think that the federal government has to put up some of the money and show some of the leadership.
I should like to illustrate one area where leadership in higher education is necessary. We do not have unlimited resources in Canada to give grants to all our universities. Universities are very expensive. Scientific training and graduate training are expensive. I do not think that every university in Canada can have a medical school or that every university in the country can have a nuclear physics department. Therefore some decision must be made as to where a given specialization should be located.
February 8, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Nugent
I think that this has to be done on some type of national basis, with the government in Ottawa giving some leadership. Yesterday the Department of Forestry and Rural Development issued a press release announcing that the department was making equal grants to the forestry faculties of the University of New Brunswick, Laval University, University of Toronto and the University of British Columbia. These happen to be the only four schools of forestry in Canada. Perhaps they are all we need, I do not know; but this is the sort of thing with which some federal authority has to concern itself.
We are not going to make very much progress, Mr. Speaker, if we keep surrendering any possible leadership which can be shown here to the provinces. Ten provincial systems of education-and again I specify university education-do not add up to a national system. It seems to me that we are going to fall very much behind other countries which have shown some type of national concern.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the situation in the United States where the constitutional position is almost the same. It is generally recognized that the predominant authority in education in the United States is in the hands of the individual states, and they run the elementary and secondary schools. But the United States federal government has set up a federal office of education which allocates funds in very great amounts to universities throughout all the states, and as far as I can determine no great objection is taken to this. I hope that before too many years pass we will think this situation through and try to reverse the unfortunate decision taken by the present government last fall after the Conference with the provinces.
My last point, Mr. Speaker, is that I do not think there would be very great objection to a similar proposal on the part of most provinces. If we do have to make a special case let us admit the fact, and make special provision for whichever province may object.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks today in a manner that always gives me the greatest pleasure. I should like to thank the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) for his courtesy in making it possible for me to be heard now, rather than himself. One of the more pleasant aspects of being a member of this house is that a political adversary, in recognizing a certain situation, can make a kind gesture of friendship such as
[Mr. Prittie.l
this. I offer my heartfelt thanks, and I am grateful.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I am pleased to have the floor at this time because today, from Edmonton, a distinguished group sits in Mr. Speaker's gallery. They are distinguished because they show that spirit that I am proud to think is Edmonton's. These people are dressed in the Klondike garb of the gay '90's. They bring to Ottawa a little of the spirit of Edmonton.
The National Surveyors Association has decided for the first time that it will hold its convention elsewhere than in Ottawa. It will hold the convention in Edmonton. In honour of this, our good friends in the gallery have the spirit to visit this city. This is something which must be encouraged.
They have brought down Klondike Kate; in fact, 26 charming people have come down. The men are dashing, gallant and handsome; the ladies beautiful, charming and gracious. I deny that these people were hand picked for these qualities; they form only a cross-section of Edmonton. If you visit our city you will find our streets filled with such beautiful, charming and gracious people.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let's go.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I also want to thank hon. members of the house for their courteous consideration, for that spontaneous parade staged around the dining room today. It was not done for advertising. Because so many of my friends were interested in seeing the beautiful girls, I asked them to walk around, that my friends for a few moments might see what I enjoy so much always in Edmonton.
I am afraid, having spoken so kindly in the house, that I shall now have to fire a few volleys I have saved over a considerable period. Having spoken kindly of everybody, I shall now revert to my normal self. At times I might sound critical, and when my hon. friends on the other side hear me, it might occur to them that they have made mistakes. If I enlarge on their errors, it simply means that those errors may be more fundamental than hon. members on the other side realize. What I have to say involves the Canadian people. If I complain about this institution, about parliament, which hon. members opposite do not seem to understand, it is because of what the Liberal government is doing to Canada.
February 8, 19G7



The whole country is concerned about where it is going. Some of us are more concerned with this question than others. I, for one, cannot understand these commissions inquiring into the status of women, or into our two languages-I refer to the B and B Commission. What utter balderdash they are. Nobody married needs to be educated about the status of women. Anybody with half a brain in his head knows he has to learn two things quickly: to say "Yes, dear" when she is right, and "Yes, dear" when she is wrong. That is the situation a man has to cope with, and it needs no royal commission to tell him that. That is the situation existing.
I do not care how many reports the B and B Commission brings in, they will not help me to learn French. I shall learn far more French by meeting one of those charming ladies from Hull, Edmontons' twin city.
There are no difficulties between English and French speaking Canada. That question I settled long ago. I have a secretary from Quebec, and when I do anything wrong she tells me. She can straighten me out more effectively than any B and B Commission could.
Our charming people from Edmonton display the Canadian spirit in a way that makes us all in this country proud to be Canadians. They are prepared to travel over Canada, to the United States and to Europe advertising the existence of their city and its charms. So long as we have people like that we need not worry about who Canadians are. Canadians are individuals. A Canadian is that type of individual with the gumption to be what he wants to be. He respects his neighbour's right to be the kind of Canadian he wants to be. Who wants people stamped from a pattern? Who are those who say that Canadians should be recognizable, by our friends across the pond and by our neighbours to the south, as coming from a distinct pattern? The greatest compliment that can be paid to us is that we are not typed, not stamped. Because you can go anywhere in the world and be recognized as an individual is the greatest compliment anybody can pay you.
We have the heritage of free speech in our democratic society. We have the right to be individuals. Are these not the objectives of our society? Who are those people so afraid of being themselves? Who is afraid of not being recognized, of not being taken for a Canadian. What is wrong with us? Is it that fear in the atomic age has strenghtened the herd instinct. Has the danger in the world herded us together? Why is there this unreasoning fear
The Budget-Mr. Nugent that we shall not be recognized as Canadians? I tell you, Mr. Speaker, when the time comes that Canadians can be picked out of a crowd, when other people can say that a Canadian does this, is this, and behaves this way, I shall leave. I shall not put up with that.
I am proud of being a Canadian. I have nothing against the United States-I have many excellent friends, first cousins, in many states, and many acquaintances in that country. But I would rather be a Canadian, because here we are individuals. The individuality of the Canadian is something our neighbours envy.
In our society we have ten times the freedom that conventional types of men have. Conventionally stamped men are so restricted that they cannot appreciate the freedom of being an individual. That is the freedom I appreciate in Canada. That is what I hope every Canadian student, growing up in our land, will appreciate, care for, and cherish.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There are actions which are taken for the right motives, but which are distrusted because they are done in the wrong way. I am sure we are all familiar with one illustration which I might use in this connection; there are some people who can tell a joke well, and others who simply cannot do so. This is all I have to say by way of introduction to my next thought, which concerns the way in which this government operates. The manner in which a thing is done is just as important as the object which is being sought. I made the same observation during the flag debate. Perhaps on reflection hon. members sitting opposite will come to understand the importance of doing things the right way. Mr. Mackenzie King began with a committee of about 20 members. He gave them unlimited time, told them the government would agree with whatever the committee decided, and the result was unanimity in the committee, except for one member. Then Jean Lesage said: "If you accept that decision I will destroy the Liberal Party in Quebec." So the government could not go any further.
By contrast, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made a political football of the issue from the start. Only after fighting positions had been taken did he refer the matter to a committee. As a result, the flag which was introduced is still associated in the minds of far too many people with the cavalier and idiotic way in which it was imposed. There-are political overtones. It is a Grit flag, rather
12804	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Nugent than the unifying symbol which the government said Canada would be given.
How can we in this country accomplish anything if decisions are to be taken in this way? Those who wanted to change the national flag may have been in a majority in Canada. Those of us who did not think a change was necessary were certainly prepared to follow the majority, if change was what they wanted. There is no doubt that the majority of Canadians wanted to be proud of that flag; they wanted a national symbol around which to rally. And there is no doubt that the majority of Canadians were sadly disappointed by the manner in which the change was brought about.
I am afraid that what the government is doing through the commission on bilingualism and biculturalism is having the same disturbing effect. It has never been my belief that differences can be healed by talking about them, rather than by curing their causes. If I have a quarrel with my neighbour there is no point in having a discussion as to how we express ourselves in our quarrel. But this is what the B and B commission is doing. We need to find out what it is that French Canadians resent about us in the west, and what we in the west resent about French speaking Canadians.
I suggest that despite a lack of understanding, due in part to an exaggerated importance being given to symbols, there is, in fact, complete identity of purpose between the province of Quebec and western Canada as to what both wish Canada to be. When I was in Quebec city, I found the people there living a western mode of life, if I may be excused for expressing myself in that way. Their hospitality was overwhelming-the kind of hospitality we talk about in the west but do not always find.
They were French but, if they will forgive me for saying so, they thought like westerners, and when I heard their complaints about Canada they reminded me very much of the expressions westerners used back in the 'thirties about "Bay Street crooks" hogging all the money, while we did not have enough to go around. There are one or two things which are basically wrong and which affect relations between French speaking and English speaking Canada. In the province of Quebec the ordinary labourer is paid less than his counterpart across this country, and the Quebec farmer generally receives a lower

DEBATES	February 8, 1967
income than do farmers elsewhere. Our problem, then, is very simple and its solution is: monetary justice for Quebec.
When this party formed the government it was supported by a very large number of members from western Canada. We still have most of them, thank God. But I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that those members from western Canada were realists. They were not unduly concerned about symbols. They wanted legislation which would put some bread on the table and ensure a few of the amenities of life for the people they represented. They wanted legislation which would put some money in their pockets and lead to a better standard of living. And that was the legislation which was brought in.
I do not want to be too critical of our French colleagues but I am afraid they were not as persuasive as they might have been. They spent too much time in the discussion of symbols, such as cheques written in both official languages. There was not forthcoming from that group in the house the necessary flow of suggestions for increasing the economic wealth of the province of Quebec.
I will admit that we did not do the great job for Quebec that we did for the rest of Canada. We did a good job for western Canada, though, and this did help all of Canada. I cannot blame the citizens of Quebec who say: Lord, how long must we wait for our turn; we are being discriminated against. It is not discrimination against Quebec. But the man whose family is going short of the amenities of life cannot be expected to appreciate the distinction between failure by intent, and failure with the best of intentions. He is not likely to be impressed by people who say: We will give you a flag and make you feel more Canadian.
I had not intended to be vehement on this subject, but I want my hon. friends from western Canada to understand something which I believe they have so far failed, to some extent, to appreciate. When you yourselves find that things are getting along much better, when westerners engaged in farming and in industry now have a real opportunity to reap a good return for their labour, it is harder to realize that there are areas in this country which are not so favoured. When the disagreement or the unhappiness in Quebec is expressed by way of symbolism that we in the west cannot understand, it leads to a widening of misunderstanding between various parts of the country. I know that French
February 8, 1967

Canadians are exactly the same type of Canadians as the western Canadians, but the people in western Canada do not know it, and the people in Quebec do not know it because we have had so much talk about the symbols, so much talk about the side effects and the politics of it.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
As I have said before in this house, it is as simple as this: the people of Quebec want simple justice. You take away that core that gives them a solid complaint and then there is nothing to exaggerate on; give them simple justice, and the rabble rousers, the separatists and unreasonable people will get no audience whatsoever.
There is no basic difficulty of Canadianism between Canadians, but there is that one problem which we shall always have to watch, and the solution is a matter of simple justice. What the Conservative government did for western Canada, the pieces of legislation we brought in that were so helpful to raise the standard of living out there, must be matched for Quebec in legislation by the federal government. I cannot believe that any amount of handouts, any raise in pensions, or any raising of grants is going to do anything to help solve this problem.
I am proud to be a Canadian and the reason I believe I am like my French Canadian friends is that they do not want handouts. They do not want assistance. They only want justice. All they ask of the government is: Quit giving us pensions; quit giving us commissions and assistance; give us simple justice; give us a chance to earn that kind of living which hard work and our native ingenuity can provide and we will be very happy to say we are all equal Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I could end on a happier note than to hope the house will agree with those last words of mine.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the kind words from the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) I rather hesitate to confess that in actual fact, since the lovely young ladies are sitting directly above him, I was trying to catch their eye and had nodded my head to them, not knowing he had been asking me for my consent to speak before me. Thus I accommodated the hon. gentleman; but I think I would do it again.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has left the chamber. I was going to congratulate him on his tenacity for remaining throughout
The Budget-Mr. Otto the debate, although many of the subjects touched upon have had little to do with his department. However, I wish to talk about some points which I think will be of interest to all Canadians, and especially to the minister's department, when it comes to the preparation of the financial items to be presented in the main budget.
By and large, Mr. Speaker, I believe we all recognize that for the next few years we are going to be concerned with the repatriation of our industrial destiny. I am not concerned with the amount of control, as is the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gordon), and neither are Canadians in general, because control is really an ambiguous thing. I believe Canadians are concerned with the goodies, the dividends, the profits. These are the things they want; and it is no great mystery, because anywhere one goes throughout Canada he cannot help noticing the great mountains of raw materials (we have.
It is no secret that we Canadians have a monopoly of uranium. It is an obvious fact that we have a seaway running into the middle of our country. We have the Churchill Falls project now developing. We are rich in hydro power and fresh water. In short, we have an advantage but are troubled that we cannot use it, that we cannot get dividends and profits from it. We know this advantage is being developed, but we also know we do not appreciably share the benefits of it, especially when we compare ourselves with countries like Germany and France, where the action is, but which do not have half the resources that we possess.
This is the problem that concerns Canadians. It is the problem that concerns the cabinet. It is the problem that concerns the Liberal party. We have these good intentions, but the problem is that we could be described as a government of innocence-

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-a government of innocence, in the sense of people who are innocent, who could be naive and fail to face the realities of life. It might be said that with our good intentions we may even be paving the road to oblivion. As the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona said, good intentions are not enough: We have to face reality. We cannot be naive. We have to be slightly cynical. We have to be realists. This is the problem that faces us with respect to control of industry or repatriation of our industry.

February 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Otto
We know that 67 per cent of our industrial strength belongs to foreigners. We also know that about 80 cents out of every dollar invested in mines goes to promoters' profit and only 20 cents, if that, goes into the ground. Recent history has shown us that when we try to get Canadians enthused about buying into Canadian companies, something like the Prudential collapse or the Atlantic collapse happens. We run into problems like that of the Western Bank and the Mercantile Bank.
There is a deep rooted problem which must be solved before we can accomplish what we are trying to accomplish. Even if we had the Canadian Development Corporation and got people convinced that they should buy into Canadian industry, and even if the Minister without Portfolio, with all his restrictive measures, could force Americans to throw their shares on to the stock exchange like confetti, nobody will pick them up because of a fundamental weakness at the stock exchange and the security exchange level.
This is where we have failed. In this area we have said that the responsibility under the B.N.A. Act is given to the provinces. The blame is placed on an antiquated piece of paper, which no one has any faith in, but the provisions of which have been overcome many times. In actual fact the B.N.A. Act will permit us to do anything.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We have been able to pass hospital insurance legislation. We have passed the pension legislation, medicare, and assistance to education. We know what has to be done in this regard and I will venture to suggest-and I hope the minister gets the message-how it can be done. We must clear up this whole stock exchange fiasco. We cannot expect Canadians to put in good money and have it disappear into great mansions on Post Road in Toronto, great palaces in Bermuda, yachts, and so on. In other words, we must convince Canadians that if they invest a dollar in a Canadian company they will receive a return. They must be assured that that money will go into the industry, or into the ground, and not into someone's pockets. This is the first task which faces us.
We have already heard about the Canada Development Corporation. I do not think it will be successful if the corporation buys up shares and then tries out some method of distributing them. I think Canadians are so security conscious now, as they should be after the experiences they have had, that they want some stamp of guarantee. You know, we

do this in respect of mortgages. We have a National Housing Act and are trying to get Canadians to invest in bricks and mortar. We guarantee this: We say that if you put in $1,000 you will get it back. So, naturally we are great mortgage investors. But, when it comes to shares and equities, we are not yet becoming involved, but there is no reason why this cannot be done.
I would have introduced a private member's bill in such a way that the Canadian Development Corporation would ensure the purchase price of shares of approved companies. This is not so radical as it may seem. It is done every day. This is the job of the commercial banker. If you have a thousand shares of General Motors, General Electric, or any shares, and go to a commercial bank, they will insure them for you. The only thing is that you have to deal with million dollar lots, and a small investor cannot take advantage of that insurance. So we must make provision for this. In that way, without going to the stock exchanges and the provinces telling them that they must abide by our regulations, we can accomplish exactly the same thing by stipulating which companies will be approved by the corporation, and which shares will be approved for insurance. In that way we could control the administration of these stock exchanges.
There is the matter of the prospectus. I am sure you have read many Canadian prospectuses. You can put just about anything in them, so long as it is true. You do not include in them the fact that there is no gold in this particular moose pasture. All you say is that Dr. Jones, a famous geologist, says that in such and such an area of Tanganyika they have found 90 per cent gold, and this type of thing. They have a perfect right to do this, and this is how we get hoodwinked. If you have ever seen the United States prospectuses, especially those filed with the Securities Exchange Commission, you will know that they are not allowed to do this. It is practically a matter of true and false: Is there gold or is there no gold; what is the company's future and what is not the company's future. What we must do in our regulations, before we approve of these shares which will come within the Canadian Development Corporation, is say that we will not take them unless the prospectus follows a certain pattern and is absolutely factual.
Then, there are the financial statements. We should be able to approve of the financial statements. We do not want to see at the bottom of them a statement by the accountant
February 8, 1967

to the effect that the information supplied is only from documents given to him and therefore that he does not accept responsibility for them. Every chartered accountant firm, or any person who is doing the accounting for a public company which wants to be approved, must say that he guarantees the particulars as of that date. Then you would find there would be a big change and that we would not get into as many of these Prudential and other messes as we have.
Now, let us take the directors of the companies. In the United States, and in fact in most countries where there are successful industries and successful corporate structures at least 50 per cent or 51 per cent of the directors of the companies make their money from the companies. In Canada, except for the president, none of the directors depend on the company for a living. Some very strange disclosures came out last night in the evidence of Mr. Stevens of Westbank. He said that one of the plums of a directorship in any Canadian bank is the right to borrow about $10 million from that bank. This is what the directors are there for. They do not know the banking business, they do not know the construction business and they do not know the manufacturing business. I would say they are professional directors-the elite; they are very conservative and very cautions. How do they make their money? They make their money on the subscription of the shares, because they have control over when the shares will be issued, and by that time they have sold their own.
So, one can see that we have a faulty mechanism. If we insist, before the shares of a company are acceptable to the Canadian Development Corporation, that at least 51 per cent of the directors are internal directors, sales managers, production managers, and so on, then you would have people who would depend on that company and on that industry for a living. We would also have to simplify the procedures. There is no reason that it should cost about $250,000 or $300,000 to put a company on the stock market. By the time you get through with the bonus shares, rights and privileges, there is very little left. Out of $4 million that the investors put in, only $2 million, after the promotion costs, winds up in the treasury of the company and with this the company must try to make a profit to pay the $4 million invested. This is something which must be remedied.
Then, there is the shareholders register. I do not know whether or not anyone has ever
The Budget-Mr. Otto tried to contest the directorship of a company. The inside directors know exactly who the shareholders are and, at the expense of the company, they can send out proxies to all the shareholders and, since most of the shareholders send them back, they are in control. But if you are a shareholder and want the list of shareholders, you must give six months' notice, pay the cost, which sometimes is about $18,000, and then by the time you get it is six months behind and therefore is useless to you. You can, however, buy a directorship of a company; it is practically on the market.
This must not continue, because we will not be successful in any of our efforts in respect of the Canadian Development Corporation or in respect of getting Canadians to purchase the shares in companies unless we get this straightened away. The way in which to do it is to set up regulations with which the companies must comply before the government will accept them into the Canadian Development Corporation, and put its stamp of approval on them. When you have done that, no company will be able to opt out of this, because if they do no one will buy the shares. They will all come in; and if all the companies come in, then you will have exactly the same regulations you would have if you change the security exchange commissions.
There is no excuse at all for the government saying "Oh, we would like to do it but we cannot because of the British North America Act". The most overrated piece of dead fish I have ever heard of or read in my life is the British North America Act. It was devised at a time when we were worried about the American invasion. This was 100 years ago, when the provincial and federal rights were absolutely different from what they are now, and even the responsibilities. If we take the initiative first and do this, we can get around it, and no one will contest it; because after all Canadians, regardless of where they live, do not give a darn whether it is a provincial right or a federal right. They do not even know it. They are disgusted to know that they are electing provincial members and federal members in order that they can sit down and fight with each other.

The hon. gentleman made an important statement when he said "at that time". The gentlemen who drafted the agreement are dead, and they had no idea what Canada was going to be like today. I do not blame the British government at all, and I have not said that I do. I said that this was a dead piece of fish as far as we are concerned. I do not understand this continual harping about inherited privileges and responsibilities. To suggest that we have certain rights because our ancestors did something is one thing, but the question is what are we going to do today. That is the situation we must face.
The federal government is at this time responsible for the canal systems. This was perhaps necessary for defence purposes, but I do not understand why canal systems should now be under federal jurisdiction. I think we would be better off if they were under provincial jurisdiction.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would not help us.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am suggesting that we should disregard the act and take the initial steps, because we want Canadians to buy shares in their companies. We must admit that even if the United States gave us the shares we probably would not accept them because basically we are not share buyers. We are cautious and apprehensive because our money has come to us the hard way, through sweat and saving. The only money which is invested in shares is money come by easily. Money received from dividends will be reinvested, and we need that kind of money. We must induce Canadians not to put their money into bricks and mortar and not to buy mortgages or perhaps even government bonds. Let us sell our bonds to the United States, because we want Canadians to buy equity. Equity grows and brings dividends and profits. These profits can be used for further industrial expansion.
The only way we can accomplish this is by providing some sort of guarantee, and this will not work unless we clean up this whole investment field. One cannot expect good results from good intentions if the basis is wrong. Let us make sure the basis is right. We must acknowledge that in spite of what we do we must have a clearinghouse. Canadians must be able to buy equity through a Canadian clearinghouse; but as

long as the rules of such a clearinghouse allow corruption, corruption will take place. The result will be that Canadians will lose faith and we will not accomplish what we are trying to accomplish.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was intrigued by the assertion of the hon. member who has just taken his seat that we have a government of innocents. He implied that the government has not been able to deal with all the problems which have faced this country because they are innocent. The hon. gentleman has not been here as long as many members on the government front benches, but let me tell him that I recall when they sat on this side of the house and said they had all the answers to our problems. At the time the previous administration was laying the foundations for the prosperity we are now enjoying, hon. members now sitting on the government side travelled from one end of this country to the other claiming they had all the answers, and belittling the foundations for prosperity then being placed on the statute books.
This government of innocents has brought about the highest cost of living, the highest interest rates, the tightest money policy and the highest burden of debt on the individual, municipal, provincial and federal governments in the entire history of this country.
This government of innocents has created a situation in which our balance of payments is almost greater than at any other time in our history. We have a trade deficit in spite of our rising exports. Perhaps what is worse is the declining influence of this nation in the councils of the world. One must also keep in mind the labour unrest which has developed in this country in the last two years. We should also consider the number of bankruptcies and financial finaglings that have taken place furing the last two years. We must then look at those innocents opposite and ask ourselves why they did not do something during the period they have been in office to come to grips with the problems which have faced Canadians.
Only a few short years ago when those gentlemen were on this side of the house they said the pigeonholes were filled with answers to the problems of this nation. These pigeonholes are still filled, because this government has failed to supply those answers, and bring forward legislation to solve our problems.
In this centennial year, three years after the government came into office, we find the present Minister of Finance, (Mr. Sharp) still
February 8, 1967	COMMONS
faced with problems of bankruptcy, and that there are other serious problems faced by individuals in our society who are trying to find a place in this country and do something to make this the nation it should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Just think how much more prosperous it is.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the minister believes that the highest consumer debt in the history of this country represents prosperity, then let him laugh and point to that with pride. If he thinks the highest interest rates in the history of our country is something to laugh about, then let him laugh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am pleased about the lower rate of unemployment.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

What is the government opposite doing to solve these problems? They are the ones who said the pigeonholes were filled with answers. The government has set up one royal commission after another to study these serious problems, but in the past several years they have not attempted to find a solution to them. Most of the measures adopted by the government have been window dressing.
I remember when the minister brought his budget in some months ago. Apparently at that time he did not think it would be necessary to bring in a mini-budget. At that time he pointed out the unemployment figures to show how they had gone down, but he does not talk about the unemployment situation today. In my hand I have a copy of the Ottawa Citizen of February 8 which indicates that unemployment is increasing. I do not intend to read the figures, but this is another indication of what has happened as a result of the careless administration of the government opposite.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
A great deal has been said about the housing situation in Canada. I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) upon sponsoring a series of seminars
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden
in this country. I had the privilege of attending one held at Regina, the capital city of Saskatchewan. At that seminar the Minister of Labour contradicted himself in much the same way this government has contradicted itself on so many occasions. When the question of the 11 per cent sales tax and its effect on the cost of housing in this country was brought up by one of the contractors at that meeting, the Minister of Labour had the audacity to suggest that, after all, there was no reason why there should not be a tax on building supplies, since there was a tax on everything else. He forgot the important objective of successive governments in this country, to try to do something with regard to the provision of a measure of housing development which would take care of the needs of the new Canadian families which are continually entering our labour markets. When I look at what this government has done with regard to housing and when I think of this 11 per cent sales tax, I cannot help but feel that it has almost destroyed the hope of the young people in this country to own a home and build a future for themselves in the years when they will be raising their families. The Minister of Finance can laugh if he wants to, but I notice he is not laughing now because he knows it is true, and he acknowledged this in the budget last spring when the government decided to remove progressively the sales tax which they had put into effect.
I ask through you, sir, why the government does not go all the way and remove this tax at this time, so as to restore to those who wish to purchase a house some equity in their purchases. After all, these are people who need housing. All I can say to the Minister of Labour with regard to his statement today, that he will reduce the rent by $16 a month, is that this reduction in the monthly payment for rentals does not even cover the increased cost that had been put into effect by the action taken by the government through the 11 per cent sales tax, alone. I want to say to you, sir, that this apparently innocent government since it came to office has cost the individual householder and the individual family in this country a great deal of money.
I wish to speak now about the sales tax on production machinery and building supplies. I believe that in his speech on December 19 the minister estimated that the raising of the sales tax by 1 per cent would bring in revenues of approximately $155 million a year.

I think it is more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If I were sitting in the minister's seat and had his responsibility I would be able to answer that question a lot better than the minister. After all it was his government which brought in the tax two and a half years ago, and then two and a half years later had to withdraw it progressively because of its effects on our economy. When this tax was brought in we on this side of the house warned the government of the dangers of inflation and of the problems involved in the increasing cost of living and the increasing cost of industrial production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Look at what we inherited.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And what did the members on the opposite side say about our warnings? Mr. Speaker, you will recall that they almost called us the enemies of society because we dared to think that anything they would do would endanger the livelihood of the Canadian people. What has happened has been almost exactly what we had forecast, except that it was far more serious than we on this side of the house indicated at that time.
I recall suggesting during that budget debate that the former minister of finance should resign. I recall the vote that followed and the fact that the members of the New Democratic Party in this House of Commons sat in their seats voicelessly when the crucial vote came. They share with the government opposite part of the responsibility for the high cost of living we are experiencing today, for the inflation and for the danger that it presents to the institutions of this country. What happened to the sense of responsibility of the members of that party sitting in opposition, when they remained silent on that issue and refused to vote on a matter which has brought to vast numbers of Canadians an

increased cost of living, as well as privation and suffering? This is something that I will never be able to understand. I do not understand how a party which puts humanitarian-ism first could have taken the action which the New Democratic Party took on that day and in this way denied the very existence of those people whom they claim to represent here in the House of Commons. I am referring to people with limited income.
However, there are other factors which enter into the financial picture in this country. One of those is the lack of incentives in agriculture. When I look at the decreasing production of some of our dairy products and the resultant reduced take-home pay of many of our agricultural people I cannot help but wonder what this government has been thinking of in this regard. I know that the former minister of agriculture said: The Conservatives had a good agricultural policy. However, I suggest to you, sir, that any policy, whether agricultural or other, cannot stand still in this country, in view of the changing situation which is taking place on a daily basis throughout this country. If we do not improve the legislation which is brought forward from time to time, we cannot hope to cope with the problems which face our people.
This brings to my mind our defence expenditures and the fact that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) refused in this house to give information on one of the most vital changes in our armed services that has ever been considered by the House of Commons. I believe that Canadians are concerned about the money that is going into defence expenditures today, because it represents approximately 25 per cent of our tax dollar. There are some people who believe that the best way to economize is to say no, and there are people who believe that real economy is to spend money judiciously and to do the job that has to be done without unnecessary frills. As I survey the plans which have been put forward by the government in this regard, I cannot help but feel that the result of their policies can only endanger Canada's position in the realm of external affairs.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
You, sir, know that there are other problems that face this nation. The economic problems are great and every member on the other side wants to call himself innocent, but he realizes the government has the machinery at its disposal, the studies that have been made, and if they wanted to come to grips with the economic problems they could act.

This has been one of the significant failures of the government-the failure to act, the failure to make a decision when that decision was right. This has been followed by a period of deterioration which destroyed a part of the heritage of the Canadian people. We face a situation in this country today when this failure is more significant than it ever was before, particularly when we consider the minister's reversal with regard to the problem of research.
Canada is an exporting nation. All of the nations of the world, and many of them are older than we are, are spending tremendous sums of money on research. Here in Canada, a nation with untold undeveloped resources, we have adopted the reversal of that attitude which has been taken by many other countries around the world. Canada should be putting millions and millions of dollars more into research than any other nation in the world. We have tremendous natural resources. The hon. member who spoke before me referred to them, and was worried about who was going to own them. Well, if we do not undertake any research to develop these resources for this nation, we are not going to be able to own them or to develop them. We will have to depend upon outside interests. I think that is a trend that cannot help but trouble the average Canadian, and which I cannot help but deplore.
The significant fact is that today we are discussing the mini-budget. I recall when this minister became the Minister of Finance. He was going to solve all the problems this nation had, and even when he presented the budget last spring-

Canadians are worried about the financial institutions of this country. I am not referring to the ones that seem to be in trouble at the moment or to those that were making he news a few months ago. I wonder what their contribution to a debate of this type would have been, with a government such as we have at the present time? We have had references to the Bank Act, and the position taken by the minister. This position has driven interest rates up, and has encouraged interest rates to rise more rapidly than at any other time. This is one of the things for which this Minister of Finance will be remembered-the highest interest rates in Canadian history and the tightest money in Canadian history. This Minister of Finance will not even rise to the bait; he will not even defend himself against these charges, because he knows they are true. I do not have the report with me, but I remember it very well. I recall that the minister of finance of that day placed the statement on the record of the House of Commons during his budget remarks. I believe most members of the house recall that very well.
When we speak of prosperity in Canada today, let us not forget that a great deal of credit for that prosperity must be given to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). During those difficult years, when we assumed the mantle of responsibility, after the people of this country threw out the Liberals, the hon. member for Ontario brought into being a vocational training program that resulted in the construction of a great number of vocational training schools across this country. I have read in the press not only of Canada but of the world that this was the greatest training program of its kind to be found anywhere. It is a tribute to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) that he had the inspiration and the vision to bring it about. Thousands of Canadians are able to work today because they are trained and are able to meet the

challenge that industry and a modern age presents. I recall, Mr. Speaker, that when we on this side of the house formed the government hon. members opposite attacked the program as being something which was too little and came too late. Yet it has been hailed the greatest program of its kind in the entire world at any period.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The hon. member who preceded me made some remarks about the British North America Act and I think I should say something in this regard, though I had not planned to. I believe he said that it was an antiquated piece of paper which no one believes in anyway; and he called it an overrated piece of dead fish. This statement comes from a member of the Liberal party, a party which believes in the rights of the provinces and in a united Canada, a party which says it stands for national unity in this 100th year of confederation. Yet no one rose on that side of the house to deny that statement.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps all of us in this house believe that the British North America Act can be improved upon. All of us would like to see the provinces get together to restate and to re-emphasize the unity of purpose that existed in 1867. But I think the remarks of the hon. member that this founding paper of our nation is an antiquated piece of paper which no one believes in anyway, that it is an overrated piece of dead fish, are an insult not only to the members of this house but to people in every part of Canada.
The year 1967 is the centennial celebration of the founding of our nation and gives us an opportunity to re-establish the purpose of Canadian life, to re-emphasizs the role of the individual in our society, to create opportunities and incentives that will give to all of us a vital, living part in the development of our nation, and to reward individual effort. I am glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will present centennial awards to Canadians, because I believe we pay far too little attention to the achievements that Canadians are able to chalk up in private life, in the university and scholastic field, and also in industry and labour. I do not think it is any denial of the status of a free people to show appreciation to those who have made an achievement; to single them out and set them on a pedestal so that others may try to accomplish similar achievements.
