Mr. Speaker, for over a year now the federal government has been trying to sustain the present economic expansion, which is now entering its seventh year. This is the longest period we have ever known in peacetime. With sound administration, there is no reason to believe a recession must inevitably follow the present period of prosperity in the country.
On the other hand, if we allow certain pressures to increase, if we do not try to relieve them, prices and costs will become excessive. Capital expenditures will become too great and a period of digestion or indigestion will follow.
The government is trying at present to reduce capital expenditures in order that Canada's long-term needs may be met without causing violent fluctuations, and our present capacity to satisfy capital expenditures may not be exceeded by demand.
In its second annual review, the Economic Council of Canada shows how company investments can become a factor of instability in the economy of our country;
Declines and expansions in investment have historically been an important factor contributing to the unstable and uneven growth of the Canadian economy.
The council then goes on to point out that although
-the actual volume of such investment will need to continue to expand considerably from current levels if potential output is to be attained in 1970-
-the recent rate of expansion in investment spending is clearly not sustainable on a long-term basis to 1970 and beyond.
The council suggests that any program aimed at stabilizing expansion,
-must endeavour to encourage a growth rate of business investment related as closely as possible to the potential growth in production.
That is why the council recommends
-that serious consideration be given to the possibility of putting off or staggering certain important building projects in areas where a lack of manpower and other resources is particularly serious.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has accepted these recommendations. In fact, in August 1965, steps had already been taken to
The Budget-Mr. Guay prevent excessive accumulation of investments. When the government took this position in August, 1965, not to mention the measures regarding its own investments and those providing assistance to the provinces and municipalities in staggering their programs, it was already asking others to do the same.
The measures announced in last year's budget speech shore up this policy which consists in deferring clearly excessive investment demands, so as to ensure stable and continued expansion.
Three complementary measures have been designed so as to supplement each other.
The measure concerning depreciation, under which businessmen can claim a lower abatement for capital costs with regard to a certain type of assets in the next three years, if they make investments in the next 18 months, is designed to prompt businessmen to defer, as far as possible, their capital expenditures until the end of that period.
The purpose of the third measure providing for a 5 per cent tax on cash profits, that is, profits after taxes, principal repaid on a long term debt, in addition to capital cost allowances, depletion allowances and some other factors, is to consolidate the other two. In view of the $30,000 exemption, it is not aimed at small concerns which, on the whole, will not be paying this tax. The purpose, however, is to temporarily deprive companies of part of the available cash they might otherwise be tempted to spend on capital expenditures. As there is already a shortage of manpower and materials in capital goods industry as well as in the construction industry, any additional expenditures would inevitably bring about an increase of costs and prices due to competition between industries for manpower and materials already in short supply.
The funds remitted to the federal government will bear interest at 5 per cent per annum and will be reimbursed at any time after 18 to 36 months; this will enable the federal government to release them when pressure weakens on supplies and will allow capital investments to maintain their advance at a rate more easily supported.
The idea of a refundable tax on cash profits is entirely new. It resembles somewhat the Swedish plan intended to regulate capital expenditures. It differs in that, apart from the $30,000 exemption, all companies must pay the tax, whereas under the Swedish plan this is optional. It differs also in that the Swedish authorities did not commit themselves to a set time limit for refunding the tax. Finally, in
February 8, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey Sweden the funds may be released only for specific purposes, that is only if they are to be used in specified areas. We believe that, in Canada, our aims will be more easily achieved through the provisions we have proposed.
I should like to point out that special attention was given to the designated areas where the rate of unemployment is usually above average and where extra help is needed. The increased capital cost allowances will still apply to ventures in the designated areas which are eligible to subsidies for new capital investments, thus giving them a double advantage. The income of new manufacturing industries located in designated areas will be eligible for a three year income tax exemption plus an exemption from the 5 per cent refundable tax.
Finally, may I point out that, apart from tax exemptions the federal government will greatly help designated areas through the Area Development Incentives Act, the Rural Development Fund and the Atlantic Development Board Fund. Through all those measures, huge amounts will be spent for the development of the areas concerned.
In closing I should like to point out to the government the urgent need for building at St. Romuald, a most important industrial centre in eastern Quebec, a deep sea wharf which will permit development of the area and cut down unemployment there.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying that it has been brought to my attention that cabinet ministers, having consulted senior officials, have concluded that approximately 100 subject matters requiring legislation await passage through the Canadian House of Commons. Immediately we ask the perennial question, why is parliament so behind in its work? My general answer is this: First, in many instances we have adopted horse and buggy practices and attitudes in the electronic age; second-and I cast no aspersions on any political party-for a young nation, Canada has built into its legislative practices an incredible number of delay procedures.
Since 1867 we have had hundreds of royal commissions. Other speakers this afternoon have mentioned them. Many royal commission findings have been excellent, yet successive governments have implemented not more than 10 per cent of commission recommendations.


I am not an expert on the rules of the House of Commons. I am anything but an expert. Yet it seems that there is a general consensus in the house that many of our rules and procedures are suited more to a bygone age. We have not adopted the committees system of the United States. In Canada, governments continue to send urgent or embarrassing questions to house committees, often not for further study and clarification, but to postpone the necessity of deciding. Many members of parliament take an initial delight in saying that the committees system, as it works these days, serves a great purpose in shedding light on contemporary problems. Through the system members of parliament become profoundly aware of the detailed implications of problems.
I suppose the electors of my district hope that by spending more time in Ottawa I shall become more educated. That is not the raison d'etre, per se, for my presence in the House of Commons. To educate and shed light is not the raison d'etre of the committee system. Its real raison d'etre, as in the United States, should be to quicken the decision making process of government. But, in Canada, the committees system is another part, an added factor, of the built-in delay procedure developed in a supposedly young, pioneering nation.
What else have we done in Canada? We have developed inquiries of all kinds, some of which admittedly are useful. Contemporary problems facing big governments obviously need to be inquired into. The bigger government becomes, the more inquiries are necessary. It is obvious that individual members of parliament cannot be experts in everything. Of course we need some inquiries. Some have been useful; others merely serve to delay the decision making process.
Today we have a new phenomenon. The Minister of Labour has had, within his federal jurisdiction, one strike after another. The strike problem is extremely urgent, and the people of Canada want action. Of course we must study the problem. We can study many precedents in Sweden, and elsewhere in Scandinavia relating to problems under federal jurisdiction. But what do we do in Canada? The Minister of Labour sets up a task force to look into strikes under the federal jurisdiction.
We have a housing crisis such as we have never had before. Instead of action what do we get? We get study groups, symposiums-in plain language, part of the built-in delay
February 8, 1967

procedure of the Canadian approach to contemporary problems.
When President Kennedy came to power, the moment he talked about a task force, the urgency of the problem was denoted, and the tentacles of the White House went out into the nation. Every expert in the nation was told to apply his knowledge to the problem, to bring about as speedy a solution as possible. The experts were given a delay period within which to report. If they could not report within a specific delay period, under reasonable circumstances the president would grant an extension.
What do we do in Canada? Having had strike after strike within the federal jurisdiction the minister tells us we now have a task force. He sets a few able men at the university level to study the problem of strikes under the federal jurisdiction, yet he has allotted them no time within which to report. We hope that some time in 1968 the minister will report to the House of Commons.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In the meantime this house is faced with tremendous difficulties vis-a-vis strikes under the federal jurisdiction. So we have a new delay of verbiage built into the Canadian experience-the task force. As I have said, one of the real reasons we are approximately 100 pieces of legislation behind in our work is that we have developed horse and buggy attitudes and techniques in the electronic age. We are told that in this electronic age an instantaneous poll of public opinion can be made available on any given date about any given issue. What has this meant to leadership in the western world?
Obviously, if Churchill or Franklin Roosevelt had relied on such polls as these, Churchill would not have stood up to Hitler the way he did and Roosevelt would not have led America out of isolation into the second world war. Today's political leaders are relying more and more for guidance on poll soundings made possible through modern techniques. Instead of speeding up the decision-making processes of modern government, the new facilities are, in fact, delaying them.
Statesmanship and the art of government is just that-an art form. It is not a matter of trying to lead on the basis of poll soundings. Far too many leaders are reading the polls instead of going ahead on courses which they believe to be correct. Of course, they must read the polls; they must read them scientifically and intelligently so as to have a good knowledge of the obstacles they would face
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey when they try to "sell" their policies. But far too many cabinet ministers in this government, and far too many political leaders in the western world, are today being led by polls instead of reading the polls to make a scientific analysis of the kind of persuasion they will have to use in order to carry out programs and policies which they deeply believe will be good for the people. This is one of the reasons for the delay in the decisionmaking process in modern government.
I pause briefly, here. In 1867 the Fathers of Confederation faced certain basic problems as they tried to pull this country together. These included relations between Canada and the United States and the relationship between the French speaking and the English speaking people-federal-provincial relations, and the like. In 1967, both domestically and abroad, the same two basic problems face Canadian legislatures-the unity of our country and our relationship with our great neighbour to the south. It is my impression that we are not making progress in the solution of either of these two major problems, because of our horse and buggy attitudes in an electronic age.
I believe that one of the greatest causes of delay in our decision-making process here in Ottawa lies in the area of federal-provincial relations and constitutional reform. The buck is passed between Ottawa and the provinces while urgent issues are held up.

Why? Because we did not really improve the system of permanent consultations between Ottawa and the provinces and second-

I wish to make the task easier for the minister by suggesting a modernization in depth of our constitution. At any event, we have not modernized the Canadian constitution, and I do not want to prejudge the results of conferences that must be held with the provinces. Perhaps the British North America Act is flexible enough for our present needs; perhaps it must be amended in one way or another; perhaps it is absolutely necessary to have a new constitution adjusted to modern times, but assuredly it is high time for us to study the matter, Mr. Speaker.

What has happened in the United States where there is today a fairly good relationship between the states and the federal government? In the United States, the federal government is taking direct action on all questions affecting one important new form of government, namely metropolitan areas. Here in Canada, failure to act in terms of planning priorities, both social and economic, in conjunction with the provinces; failure to improve consultative machinery between Ottawa and the provinces, and failure to embark on the work we must do in order to

obtain a modern constitution suited to modern times means that many important contemporary problems are not being attacked by any level of government. I do not say this in any partisan way; I realize the extent of the difficulties which are involved.
What has happened in this house in the past few months? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) says we can do nothing more about the cost of living because we do not really have sufficient constitutional power. The provinces say, "That is not our responsibility, it is the federal responsibility." What is the minister in charge of C.M.H.C. saying as he goes around the country? He is saying it is really a provincial responsibility, and the provinces are saying that the federal government should take the real initiative. I contrast this with what happened in the United States. The Americans drafted their first constitution; it did not really work so they had to do the job again. We drafted the B.N.A. Act. Just this afternoon a supporter of the government suggested that we at the federal level cannot protect investors in Canada, and that the Minister of Finance was having trouble in that respect. Mr. Speaker, my remarks in this debate will be limited and perhaps a little parochial in nature. I trust that the house will bear with me. The first matter with which I should like to deal is in respect of a situation of which I am sure the minister is aware. This is something which arises from time to time. I should like to use a specific example so that the minister will understand just what it is I am speaking of. This is a case where an individual enters into what could be, and has been, construed as a business venture for gain. In the course of seeking advice from the local income tax authorities, he was left with a misunderstanding or unawareness in respect of the full extent of the application of the Income Tax Act with regard to what is and what is not taxable income. Subsequently, however, in making out his return he included information concerning certain money earned together with a computation of profits made, and so on. In other words, he made no attempt to hide a particular transaction; but in the computation of the tax payable he does not include this as taxable income.
His return is filed and, in this particular case, three years go by. Cases arise, either by way of automatic spot checks or accidentally, where certain returns are checked. In any event, this particular return was checked. It was determined that while indeed the taxpayer had been completely honest and factual in filling out his return, he failed to include this amount as taxable income. From his point of view there was justifiable reason for this. The whole matter then becomes a matter for review. The individual is persuaded that his
February 8, 1967

original interpretation perhaps was not correct or that the advice given him by his solicitor was not correct. He then pays the overdue tax. However, in this particular case he finds that he is subject to a 6 per cent penalty in respect of the intervening years when this tax was not paid.
1 am sure these are not rare cases and I am concerned about the unfortunate situation in which such persons find themselves when they are assessed this penalty. I suppose the question is, who ultimately is responsible. Is it not the responsibility of the people in the department to properly assess and check all income tax returns? Are we faced with a situation in which people are playing a game of Russian roulette? Are there hundreds of people-unlike this person who was honest in filing his return-who are playing a game of Russian roulette with the officials in the Department of National Revenue in an effort to escape paying taxes? Is this what is happening?
This has caused Mr. Fryer, to whose case I have been referring for the past few moments, grave concern. It has caused him concern to the point where he is asking pertinent and, I think, quite justifiable questions. I should like to read into the record part of a letter, so that we can understand the extent of his concern about this:
As a taxpayer I am convinced that inefficiency does exist in this department and I cannot accept the excuse that they do not check all the income tax files every year but only spot check them. It is a well known fact that the employees in this department are not overworked and never have their work up to date so with the number of employees they have and with all the latest computing machines available the checking of each file every year should be a very simple matter-
He raised numerous other points. There is no attempt on his part not to pay what it has been decided and determined by due process of assessment by the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue is due. What he objects to, after having acted honestly and in good faith, is that three years later he finds that he must not only pay the tax that is due but also this additional penalty. It seems that the attitude of the department is a mechanical one. The act says one thing and that is the way in which it is interpreted and enforced. There seems to be no capacity to absorb what in effect Mr. Frank Fryer of Halifax, in this particular case, understands not to have been his responsibility. I would hope that at some point in the near future the minister would be able to deal with this as a general problem.
The Budget-Mr. Forrestall
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise one other matter which has been of some continuing concern, I am sure, to all members from the maritime provinces. This is a very broad and general matter. It has to do with the whole field of government incentives and the approach which the government now is taking in a haphazard fashion to raise the standards of the people, and the opportunities for employment in the Atlantic region, up to some kind of an acceptable level in relation to the rest of Canada.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, unemployment in the maritime provinces now runs somewhere in the order of 10.5 per cent. Apart from the attempts of the previous government, over the last 25 years there has been absolutely nothing done in a positive or concrete way to overcome this difficulty. Depending upon the area, I understand that unemployment in Canada runs from about 3.8 per cent to 6.4 per cent. The average is only about half as high as it is in the maritimes. The government must accept a part of the responsibility for this situation, because of the shotgun approach which is currently in vogue in respect of incentives. On a number of occasions in this chamber arguments have been put forward in support of extending the area incentives program to embrace the Atlantic region. That argument has been shot down for a number of reasons, the paramount one being that it would establish a precedent which the government does not want established. That is a very short-range view, and shows a lack of imagination or intelligent approach.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
We must appreciate the extent and magnitude of the unemployment situation in the maritime provinces. The solution to this problem has been associated with incentives to increase secondary industry. As long as the government continues to follow the shotgun approach to these problems connected with industry, fishing and farming, as well as defence, power, import and export traffic, and the broad field of transportation, no lasting solution will be found. The government must adopt one concerted plan before this extremely high level of unemployment in relation to the rest of the country will be changed.
Recently we passed a massive transportation bill. Transportation is a key factor in the lifeblood of the Atlantic provinces. A good transportation system would encourage and make possible the development of viable secondary industry, and without it secondary industry cannot even locate there, let alone
February 8, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Forrestall flourish or participate in the growth of national income. At this time we are experiencing a waiting period. This is a further frustration in our attempts to bolster a sagging economy; it is a further frustration in our attempts to catch up to the rest of Canada.
We are waiting for the conclusion of a special study of maritime transportation problems. It is hoped that this special study will have embraced the entire economic spectrum of transportation and its effect upon the economy of the maritimes. If it does not, I am sure when we reach such a debate the maritime members of parliament, regardless of their political affiliation, will band together to overcome the shortcomings and shortfalls of the recommendations.
The government must apply to this whole massive problem the philosophy that in the long run it will be good for Canada to build a viable, live and prosperous Atlantic area. I am sure no one disagrees with that philosophy; yet we find ourselves unbolstered and unsupported by any co-ordinated federal activity in this field, such as that which fires the imagination of those people who have some understanding of the situation when they contemplate the proposed Fundy tidal power development project. The conversion of this tidal power to electricity is of such tremendous magnitude that in the Bay of Fundy this could provide the greatest source of waterpower on the North American continent. The potential source of electric energy is of such tremendous magnitude it could be the largest single source of hydro power on this continent, even if only a small proportion of it was tapped. What should such a tremendous source of power mean to the maritime provinces? I could not even begin to outline the economic impact that would result, or the impact that would result if a start were made on this project some time this year.
In answer to those who object to this massive development of hydro power, let me say that I do not believe this will be a complete answer to the problems of the power hungry Atlantic provinces at this time, or perhaps even in 25 to 30 years. Let me remind hon. members that at this time United States authorities have plans to expand the power capacity of the Hoover dam complex. The United States is not only prepared to go forward with this project, it is in the advance stages of doubling or tripling the power capacity of that complex at an expenditure of some hundreds of millions of dollars.

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I have no idea what it would cost the Canadian taxpayer to move into this Fundy tidal power project, but such a development would have a tremendous impact on the economy of the Atlantic provinces. We have all observed the delays in respect of the Churchill Falls development. This whole development has been a matter of attention for a considerable number of years, but we are still not using power developed there. I do not know why this is so. Many obstacles have had to be overcome. However, the point I wish to make is that it took many years to get to the stage at which we find them now. Because of these obstacles, are we not to proceed with the Fundy tidal power? We know it is a transmission route, and therefore the cost to the power-hungry centres in the northeastern United States and in central Canada, areas which are closer to it, will be a lot less. We are aware that massive investments would have to be made in order to bring this about, but if it is approached on a reasoned basis it could mean the total rejuvenation of Nova Scotia, and indeed of all the Atlantic provinces. They say that it is difficult to describe the total power potential of the tides of the Bay of Fundy.
Mr. Speaker, before I run out of time I should like to mention one other point, and this again is something that the government can do if it is not prepared to bring all of the approaches to maritime problems under one authority, and that is to take a serious look at the import-export traffic, the future of international shipping, and in particular the adequate development of the port of Halifax to absorb and accept the cargoes that will be transported by water within the very near future. Already we have seen the extension of massive ships into the bulk cargo transportation scheme, such as oil transportation. The government should be encouraging our oil industries in Canada to give consideration to the development of central depots for receiving oil from South America. It has been explained that in view of the present planning and technological developments it will always be cheaper to bring oil from South America than from the west. We are not asking for massive expenditures which would be required to put a pipe line into our area; indeed this is not what we want. We can accomplish the same thing, which would have a good effect on our balance of payments, by trading this great natural resource.
What we have to do in order to accomplish this is not only to talk about it for the next
February 8, 1967

four or five years, but to decide now to move ahead with it so that the industries and the interests that are directly concerned and involved in this kind of enterprise can themselves plan accordingly. The establishment of a central oil depot which will accommodate three, four and five hundred thousand ton bulk carriers must be considered now. We have the natural facilities in the harbour, we have the necessary depth of water and all we need is a determined decision on the part of the government to move ahead with it. It is a self-liquidating expense. I assure the minister that the cost involved would be returned much more quickly than will be the cost of the seaway.
The port of Halifax must be developed now to accept cargo ships of this magnitude. It must be designed so as to include the concept of the integral train. We must stop thinking of transportation in a dual sense; it is not. Goods moving from the source of manufacture to the source of sale must be considered as an integral transportation package. Like the Fundy power, the theory of the integral train staggers the imagination. It is a simple extension of the ship to the rail. It is the movement of cargo out of the ship and directly to a massive train which is not owned by either the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. but rather is owned by a corporate entity involved in the movement of the particular goods. It may be a consortium of interests, it may be west coast lumber interests moving lumber and lumber products into the European market, and it may be a consortium of interests which has bought the rolling stock and accepts the responsibility for everything that is involved.
Preliminary studies have demonstrated the benefits of this system of the integral train. The massive or unit train system is a slightly different concept. However, surveys have shown us that we can now accept the proposition that transportation by rail can be even cheaper than transportation by water. The salvation of the port of Halifax as a viable economic contributor to the economy of Canada depends on this. These are not rhetorical propositions. Lack of action on the part of the government can only result in a chronic unemployment situation in the mari-times. I wish the St. Lawrence would stay frozen until around 1980, at which time the government may get around to doing something about these two or three necessary developments. The number of people working on the waterfront today compared with five years ago is staggering, and the impact has

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of a retiring annuity to Governors General of Canada and to their widows.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Mcllrailh thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-265, to provide for the payment of a retiring annuity to the Governor General of Canada.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF VARIOUS ACTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF OFFICIALS

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (for Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF VARIOUS ACTS RESPECTING SALARIES OF OFFICIALS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Canada Grain Act, the Income Tax Act, the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act, the National Energy Board Act, the Railway Act, the Tariff Board Act, the Canada Elections Act, the Financial Administration Act, the Representation Commissioner Act, and the Appropriation Act No. 4, 1964, with respect to the salaries of certain public officials.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Mcllrailh thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-266, to provide for the revision of certain salaries fixed by statute.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. T. Pennell (for Minister of Justice) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING EXPENSES, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Judges Act to revise judicial salaries and certain provisions of the said act respecting the payment to judges of travelling allowances and other expenses; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
